gara-tie-dye.courseTitle: Gara Tie-Dye — Fabric Fundamentals to Professional Mastery
gara-tie-dye.courseDescription: A complete professional pathway in Sierra Leonean Gara tie-dye: from understanding cotton and indigo, through pattern design and dye chemistry, to scaling production and running an export-ready workshop.
gara-tie-dye.intro: Learn Gara tie-dyeing from the ground up — from understanding cotton and indigo to running a workshop that exports. Master the craft, then build a business around it.

learningOutcomes: Identify and select appropriate fabrics, threads, and tools for Gara production
Design and predict resist-dye patterns using traditional and contemporary motifs
Prepare and maintain indigo vats, mordants, and colour baths to a repeatable standard
Scale from single-piece production to batch runs with consistent quality
Cost, price, market, and export Gara textiles profitably

skillDomains.name: Materials & Fabric
skillDomains.description: Know your materials. Fabric choice, thread, and tool handling determine everything downstream.

skills.name: Fabric Fundamentals
skills.description: Identify cotton types, weaves, and how each takes dye.

modules.title: What is Gara?
modules.content:
Gara is the Sierra Leonean name for wax-resist and tie-dye textiles. It shares roots with Nigerian adire and sits inside the wider West African resist-dye tradition.

The technique is simple to say and hard to master: you prevent dye from reaching parts of the cloth, then dye the rest. The untouched parts stay pale. The dyed parts go deep.

Gara is not decoration. It is a language. Every pattern has a name, a history, and a message.

By the end of this skill, you will look at any cloth and know what it is, how it was made, and what it can become.

modules.title: Cotton, rayon, silk — how they differ
modules.content:
Cotton

The traditional base for Gara. Absorbs dye evenly. Durable. Locally available. Start here.

Rayon

Takes dye brighter than cotton but fades faster and can tear under heavy handling. Use for decorative cloth, not for wearables.

Silk

Luxury-grade. Rare in West African workshops because of cost. Produces stunning colour depth.

The rule

If you can only buy one fabric for your whole learning journey: 100% cotton. It forgives mistakes and rewards skill.

steps.q: Which fabric is best for a Gara cloth that must last years and be worn regularly?
steps.f: Cotton holds dye and lasts. Synthetics resist dye or fade unevenly.

steps.q: You feel a fabric that is cool, slightly rough, and when burned turns to soft ash with a paper smell. What is it?
steps.f: The burn test — natural fibres turn to ash and smell like burnt paper; synthetics melt into a hard bead.

steps.q: Which fabric takes dye the brightest but fades fastest?
steps.f: Rayon absorbs dye fast and bright but loses colour quickly under sun and washing.

modules.title: Why you must wash before dyeing
modules.content:
New fabric has sizing — a starch coating added during manufacturing to keep it crisp. Sizing blocks dye. If you dye new cloth without washing, you get uneven, pale results.

The prep routine

  1. Fill a basin with hot water and a spoon of detergent.
  2. Soak the fabric for 30 minutes.
  3. Rinse in clean water until no suds remain.
  4. Hang to dry — do not tumble.
  5. Iron flat before marking patterns.
Prep is 30% of the finished quality. Skip it and every later step fights you.

steps.q: You have just bought new cotton from the market. What is the very first step?
o: Wash in hot water with detergent
steps.f: Always wash first. Everything else comes after.

steps.q: After washing, the fabric is dry but wrinkled. What do you do before marking patterns?
steps.f: Wrinkles distort pattern marks. Iron flat while dry.

steps.q: You wash in cold water only. What is the risk?
steps.f: Cold water does not fully remove sizing. Hot water and detergent are required.

modules.title: Interactive: Layered pattern for a client
Customer wants a low-shrink cloth
modules.prompt: A customer commissions a 2-metre Gara cloth and insists it must not shrink more than 2% after washing. Raw cotton shrinks 5–10% on first wash. You have the tools and time to pre-treat. How do you prepare the fabric?
modules.context: This is a real commercial concern — export clients will reject orders that shrink beyond spec.
modules.placeholder: Describe your preparation steps in order…
rubric: Pre-wash before cutting to size
Note the expected shrink percentage
Describe how you dry (line vs tumble)
Confirm final measurement check after drying
Address any additional stabilisation step (e.g., hot wash + cold rinse)

modules.title: Interactive: Advanced commission with colour mood
Write your fabric prep SOP
modules.prompt: Create a one-page Standard Operating Procedure for preparing fabric before dyeing, usable by any workshop apprentice.
modules.context: Real workshops run on written procedures. This becomes part of your professional portfolio.
steps: List each step with clear instructions
Note equipment needed for each step
Include a quality checkpoint after each step
Add a photo or sketch of the setup

skills.name: Threads & Tools
skills.description: The needles, threads, waxes, and tools you work with every day.

modules.title: The thread matters
modules.content:
In tie-dye Gara, thread is not for sewing — it is your drawing tool. The way you tie and stitch determines the pattern.

Common threads

  • Cotton twine — strong, forgiving, works for thick folds
  • Nylon thread — thin, precise, for fine pattern work
  • Rubber bands — quick and cheap, good for beginners

Professional Gara makers keep a range of thicknesses on hand. Thin thread makes fine lines; thick thread makes bold ones.

modules.title: Your workshop toolkit
modules.content:
A serious Gara workshop needs:

  • Sharp scissors
  • Needles in multiple sizes
  • Wooden pegs or clamps
  • A large dye pot (enamel or stainless steel — never aluminium)
  • Wooden stirring stick dedicated to dye
  • Rubber gloves
  • A drying line in shade

The dye pot is the most important. Aluminium reacts with indigo and ruins the bath. Enamel or stainless steel lasts for years.

modules.title: Match the tool to its job

steps.q: You need to make fine, precise lines in a small pattern. Which tool?
steps.f: Nylon thread is thin and precise — perfect for fine lines.

steps.q: Which material must your dye pot NOT be made of?
steps.f: Aluminium reacts with indigo and metallic salts, ruining the bath.

steps.q: You're dyeing a large cloth and need to keep folds tight for a bold pattern. Best option?
steps.f: Rubber bands or heavy twine hold thick folds tightly under dye pressure.

modules.title: Three foundational tie techniques
modules.content:
1. Spiral tie

Lay the fabric flat, pinch the centre, and twist. Tie at intervals along the twist. Creates a radiating spiral pattern.

2. Fold-and-tie

Fold the fabric into a triangle or strip, then tie across the fold at regular intervals. Creates repeating geometric bands.

3. Stitch-and-gather

Run a needle and thread along a marked line, then gather tightly. Creates long, flowing lines that follow the stitching.

Practice each on a small square before applying to a full cloth.

steps.q: You want a repeating geometric band pattern across the cloth.
steps.f: Fold-and-tie creates clean repeating bands.

steps.q: You want a radiating sunburst from the centre.
steps.f: Spiral tie is the only technique that produces a radiating sunburst.

steps.q: You want long, flowing lines following a curve you've drawn.
steps.f: Stitch-and-gather follows any line you can stitch, no matter the shape.

modules.title: Build a tie-technique sampler
modules.prompt: Create a sampler of at least 5 distinct tie techniques on small fabric squares. Photograph and label each one with the technique, thread used, and expected result.
steps: Cut 5+ squares of washed cotton
Apply a different technique to each
Dye them all in the same bath for consistency
Photograph the finished sampler
Write a one-line note under each about what you learned

skills.name: Workshop Safety
skills.description: Protect your hands, lungs, and workspace. Dye work involves chemicals and dyes that demand respect.

modules.title: Why safety is a skill
modules.content:
Indigo, caustic soda, and dye fixatives are powerful chemicals. A workshop that ignores safety will eventually injure someone — usually the youngest apprentice.

Safety is not optional. It is a core professional skill. Every professional workshop you visit will have safety protocols. Learning them now is how you become employable later.

modules.title: Personal protective equipment
modules.content:
Always wear

  • Rubber gloves — caustic soda burns skin
  • Apron or old clothes — dye stains permanently
  • Closed shoes — spills happen
  • Dust mask — when handling powdered dyes

Never do

  • Eat or drink in the dye area
  • Touch your face with gloved hands
  • Work alone with caustic soda on a first attempt

steps.q: You're about to mix caustic soda into water. Which is correct?
o: Add soda to water slowly while stirring
steps.f: Always add caustic soda to water, never the reverse.

steps.q: You must handle powdered dye. What PPE is essential?
steps.f: Powdered dye can be inhaled. Mask and gloves are minimum.

steps.q: You finish dyeing and your gloves have dye on them. What do you do?
o: Rinse them in the dye pot
Peel them off by the cuff and dispose safely
steps.f: Peel gloves from the cuff inward without touching the outside.

modules.title: Handle a chemical splash
modules.prompt: An apprentice spills caustic soda solution on their forearm. They are panicking. You are the workshop lead. Walk through exactly what you do in order.
modules.context: Caustic soda burns continue until thoroughly flushed. Fast, correct action prevents scarring.
rubric: Remove contaminated clothing/gloves first
Flush with copious running water for at least 20 minutes
Do NOT neutralise with acid — flushing is the correct response
Do NOT apply creams or ointments
Arrange medical assessment
Record the incident for future prevention

modules.title: Write a workshop safety code
modules.prompt: You are opening a small Gara workshop with three apprentices. Write a one-page safety code that covers daily operations.
modules.context: Insurance, government registration, and export contracts increasingly require documented safety procedures.
rubric: Covers PPE requirements
Covers chemical handling and storage
Covers emergency procedures
Assigns responsibility (who checks what, when)
Includes a training requirement for new apprentices

modules.title: Design a workshop safety poster
modules.prompt: Design and photograph a safety poster to display in your workshop. It must be readable from 2 metres and cover the four most important safety rules.
steps: Choose the 4 most important rules
Design with clear icons and short text
Use colours that stand out
Print or hand-paint and display in your workspace
Photograph the finished poster in place

skillDomains.name: Design & Pattern
skillDomains.description: Design is what separates a craftsperson from an artist. Learn to plan patterns with intention and cultural awareness.

skills.name: Pattern Design
skills.description: Plan, sketch, and predict how patterns will look after dyeing.

modules.title: Pattern is intention
modules.content:
Every strong Gara cloth starts on paper. Not in dye.

Professional pattern design has four steps:

  1. Intention — what is this cloth for? Wearable? Wall art? Commission?
  2. Sketch — draw the layout on paper.
  3. Predict — imagine what each mark will become after dye and resist.
  4. Test — cut a small sample square and dye it before committing the full cloth.

Beginners skip the sketch and regret it. Professionals always sketch.

modules.title: Predicting the result
modules.content:
In dyeing, what you tie stays pale; what you don't goes dark. Beginners picture the opposite.

Before you tie a single knot, ask:

  • Which parts will resist dye?
  • Which parts will absorb it fully?
  • What happens at the boundary — will it be sharp or feathered?

Sharp boundaries come from tight wrapping. Feathered boundaries come from looser ties. Both are useful. Know which you want.

steps.q: You tie tightly at 5 evenly spaced points along a folded strip, then dye. What pattern appears?
steps.f: Evenly spaced ties produce evenly spaced pale bands.

steps.q: You tie loosely with thin thread. The dye bleeds slightly into the resisted area. What boundary do you get?
steps.f: Loose ties allow dye to creep in, producing a soft feathered edge.

steps.q: You want a full-coverage pattern with no visible pale areas. What approach?
o: Tie many points densely across the whole cloth
steps.f: Dense multi-point tying is how you build a busy, full-coverage pattern.

modules.title: Design for a client brief
modules.prompt: A boutique in Freetown commissions 10 Gara scarves for a spring collection. Brief: bold geometric patterns, indigo and natural white, suitable for office wear. Describe your design approach — layout, technique, colours, and how you'll test before production.
modules.context: Professional design work always responds to a brief.
rubric: References the brief (bold geometric, indigo + white, office-appropriate)
Chooses specific tie techniques that produce geometric patterns
Considers consistency across a 10-piece run
Describes a sample-test step before committing to production
Addresses production time and material estimate

modules.title: Build a pattern design portfolio
modules.prompt: Create a portfolio of at least 4 original pattern designs, each with a sketch, a sample, and a one-paragraph note explaining the intention.
steps: Sketch each pattern on paper
Produce a physical sample
Photograph sketch and sample together
Write a note: what was the intention? What worked? What would you change?
Assemble into a single portfolio document

skills.name: Cultural Symbols
skills.description: Understand the meaning behind West African patterns. Gara is not decoration — it is a language.

modules.title: Patterns carry meaning
modules.content:
Throughout West Africa, textile patterns carry meaning — proverbs, historical events, values, social status, and identity. A client commissioning a cloth for a wedding, funeral, or naming ceremony expects patterns that respect the occasion.

This is a professional skill. Getting it wrong can lose a client permanently.

modules.title: Sierra Leonean pattern traditions
modules.content:
Sierra Leone has its own resist-dye traditions alongside the wider West African vocabulary. Common motifs include:

  • Concentric circles — representing continuity and the family
  • Zigzag lines — resilience, going around obstacles
  • Diamonds — prosperity and good fortune
  • Crosshatch — community and interconnection

Always ask the client what the cloth is for. Then choose motifs that match.

modules.title: Match the motif to the meaning

steps.q: Which motif is most appropriate for a naming ceremony?
steps.f: Concentric circles evoke continuity and family.

steps.q: A client commissions a cloth for a business launch. Best motif?
steps.f: Diamonds traditionally signal prosperity and good fortune.

steps.q: Which motif represents resilience and overcoming obstacles?
steps.f: Zigzags evoke going around or through obstacles — a resilience symbol.

modules.title: Commission for a memorial cloth
modules.prompt: A family commissions a Gara cloth to be draped at a memorial service. The deceased was a respected elder known for community service. Describe the pattern, colours, and any motif choices you would make — and why.
modules.context: Funeral textiles are one of the most important Gara commissions. The wrong motif can offend the family. The right one becomes a treasured heirloom.
rubric: Uses colours appropriate to mourning (white and indigo; sometimes black)
Chooses motifs that reference community service or an elder's role
Explains the reasoning behind each choice
Considers asking the family about specific preferences
Avoids celebratory motifs inappropriate for the occasion

modules.title: Research a pattern's origin
modules.prompt: A client requests a specific traditional pattern she inherited on a cloth from her grandmother. She doesn't know its name or meaning. Describe how you would research the pattern — who you'd ask, what you'd examine, and how you'd present findings to the client.
modules.context: Cultural stewardship is part of the professional dyer's role. Getting the history right builds trust.
rubric: Identifies elders or practitioners to consult
Describes visual documentation of the pattern
Cross-references multiple sources (oral history, museum archives, existing textiles)
Presents findings respectfully to the client
Notes the difference between a tradition and a family-specific variation

modules.title: Build a personal symbol library
modules.prompt: Compile a reference library of at least 10 traditional motifs with their meanings, drawn from elders, archives, or existing Gara work in your region.
steps: Interview at least 3 elder practitioners or visit a museum
Sketch each motif
Write a short note on its meaning and origin
Assemble into a reference document you can consult with clients

skillDomains.name: Dye Chemistry
skillDomains.description: The science behind the craft. Understand indigo, mordants, and pH.

skills.name: Indigo Fundamentals
skills.description: Work with natural indigo: prepare a vat, control pH, and produce consistent colour.

modules.title: What is indigo?
modules.content:
Indigo is a natural dye extracted from the leaves of Indigofera plants — grown throughout West Africa for centuries.

Indigo is unlike other dyes. It is not water-soluble in its natural form. To dye with it, you must chemically reduce it into a soluble yellow-green state, dye the cloth in that state, then expose it to air where it oxidises back to blue.

This is why freshly dyed indigo cloth looks green when it comes out of the vat and turns blue as it dries in the air.

modules.title: The indigo vat
modules.content:
Ingredients

  • Indigo powder
  • Water
  • Reducing agent (traditionally wood ash lye or ripe fruit; industrially, thiourea dioxide or sodium hydrosulfite)
  • Alkali (caustic soda or wood ash lye)

The process

  1. Dissolve indigo in warm water with a small amount of alkali.
  2. Add the reducing agent slowly.
  3. Wait. The vat will turn yellow-green with a coppery skin on top.
  4. It is ready when it smells slightly sweet and the skin is fully formed.

A healthy vat is a living thing. Feed it, warm it, and it produces colour for months.

steps.q: Your indigo vat looks blue instead of yellow-green. What does this mean?
o: The vat has oxidised — add more reducing agent
steps.f: Yellow-green with a coppery skin is the ready state. Blue means oxidised — feed it reducer.

steps.q: Your cloth comes out of the vat green, but after 10 minutes in air it's still not fully blue. Likely cause?
o: Still oxidising — give it more time and air
steps.f: Oxidation takes 10–20 minutes. Green-to-blue is a gradual transition, not instant.

steps.q: Your vat has a foul smell and a grey scum on top. What's wrong?
steps.f: Over-reduced vats smell bad and don't yield good colour. Rebalance with fresh indigo and gentle warming.

modules.title: Fix a struggling vat
modules.prompt: You've inherited an indigo vat from a departing colleague. It's pale blue, has no coppery skin, and the cloth you test-dipped comes out pale grey. Describe your diagnostic steps and how you'd restore it to working condition.
modules.context: Vat restoration is a core professional skill. Never throw away a struggling vat — fix it.
rubric: Check temperature (should be warm, ~30–50°C)
Check pH (should be strongly alkaline — test with litmus)
Assess reducing agent level (smell test, coppery skin)
Restore systematically: warm first, then feed reducer, then indigo
Avoid over-correcting — small increments, not large additions

modules.title: Maintain an indigo vat log
modules.prompt: Create a 4-week vat log tracking every addition, every dip, and the resulting colour outcomes. This becomes a reference you can use to reproduce consistent results for years.
steps: Set up a table: date, temperature, pH reading, indigo added, reducer added, dip count, colour result
Log every vat session for 4 weeks
Photograph a fabric swatch at the end of each session
Review at the end of the month and note patterns
Identify what kept the vat healthiest

skills.name: Dye Vats & Colour Depth
skills.description: Control depth, tone, and repeatability across multiple dye baths.

modules.title: Why dip count controls depth
modules.content:
Each dip adds colour but the relationship is not linear. Two dips are darker than one — but not twice as dark. Five dips are darker than three — but only marginally.

The rule of thumb:

  • 1 dip — light, pastel
  • 2 dips — medium, wearable
  • 3 dips — deep, ceremonial
  • 4+ dips — very deep, saturation-limited

Beyond 4 dips the colour barely changes — you're wasting time and dyestuff.

modules.title: Aeration between dips
modules.content:
Between each dip, the cloth must be lifted out and exposed to air for 10–20 minutes so the indigo oxidises from green to blue.

If you re-dip too fast:

  • The colour doesn't fully develop
  • You get a muddy, uneven tone
  • The final colour is weaker than it should be

Slow down. Aeration is not optional.

steps.q: You want a light pastel indigo for a baby gift. How many dips?
steps.f: 1 dip gives a light pastel — appropriate for a gentle occasion.

steps.q: You want deep ceremonial indigo for a chief's installation. How many dips?
steps.f: 3 dips gives the deep ceremonial weight. Beyond 4 is diminishing returns.

steps.q: You dipped 6 times but the colour looks only slightly darker than 4 dips. Why?
o: Saturation limit — extra dips waste time and dyestuff
steps.f: Indigo reaches saturation around 4 dips. Extra dips give diminishing returns.

modules.title: Plan a dip schedule for 12 cloths
modules.prompt: You need to dye 12 identical table runners to medium indigo. Your vat holds 4 cloths at a time. Describe your dip schedule — how many dips, how long each dip, how long aeration, and how you handle the vat capacity limit.
modules.context: Real workshop scheduling is a constraint-satisfaction problem.
rubric: Specifies dip count (2 for medium indigo)
Specifies dip duration (consistent per dip)
Specifies aeration time (10–20 minutes)
Batches cloths to respect vat capacity (4 at a time)
Identifies total time per batch and total time overall

modules.title: Build a depth reference chart
modules.prompt: Create a permanent reference: a fabric chart showing 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5-dip indigo samples, photographed together under the same light. This becomes your standard for colour communication with clients.
steps: Cut 5 identical cotton squares
Dye each for 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 dips respectively
Rinse and dry all under identical conditions
Photograph them together in natural light
Label each with the dip count and a short description

skills.name: Mordants & Fixatives
skills.description: Understand how mordants fix colour and how to use them safely.

modules.title: What is a mordant?
modules.content:
A mordant is a chemical that binds dye to fibre. Without a mordant, many dyes wash out or fade quickly.

For indigo, the mordant is not required — indigo is a vat dye that bonds strongly to cotton by itself. But for other natural dyes (madder, turmeric, kola), mordants are essential.

Common mordants

  • Alum — most common, safe, produces clear colours
  • Iron — darkens and shifts colour ("saddening")
  • Copper — deepens greens and blues
  • Tannin — pre-mordant for cellulose fibres

modules.title: Applying a mordant
modules.content:
The pre-mordant method:

  1. Dissolve mordant in hot water (typically 10–20% of fabric weight for alum).
  2. Soak wet fabric in the mordant bath for 30–60 minutes at 60–80°C.
  3. Remove fabric and rinse lightly.
  4. Dye immediately or dry and dye later.

The post-mordant method (for some dyes) reverses this — dye first, then mordant. Follow the dye manufacturer's instructions.

steps.q: You want clear, bright colour from madder root. Which mordant?
steps.f: Alum gives the clearest, brightest results for madder.

steps.q: You want to darken and shift a colour toward a muddy tone. Which mordant?
steps.f: Iron saddens colours — darkens and shifts them toward earthy tones.

steps.q: You're dyeing cotton with a natural dye and getting weak colour. What pre-treatment do you add?
o: Tannin as a pre-mordant for cellulose
steps.f: Cellulose fibres benefit from tannin pre-treatment before alum mordant.

modules.title: Handle mordant chemicals safely
modules.prompt: You've been asked to teach an apprentice to mix and apply alum and iron mordants. Write the safety protocol they must follow at every stage.
modules.context: Iron and copper mordants are toxic if ingested or inhaled. Alum is safer but still a chemical to respect.
rubric: PPE requirements (gloves, apron, mask for powders)
Mixing protocol (add powder to water, never water to powder)
Ventilation requirements
Waste disposal (do not pour down the sink — dilute and dispose per local rules)
What to do in case of skin/eye contact
Storage requirements (sealed, labelled, out of reach of children)

modules.title: Build a mordant swatch comparison
modules.prompt: Dye 4 identical cotton swatches with the same natural dye but different mordants (alum, iron, copper, tannin+alum). Photograph side by side to show the colour shift each mordant produces.
steps: Cut 4 identical cotton squares
Mordant each with a different mordant
Dye all 4 in the same dye bath
Rinse and dry under identical conditions
Photograph together and label each

skills.name: Colour Mixing
skills.description: Combine dyes to produce new tones and match client requests.

modules.title: Three primaries, many colours
modules.content:
Every dye artist mixes from a small set of primary dyes. For natural dye work, common primaries are:

  • Indigo — blue
  • Madder — red
  • Turmeric or weld — yellow

Mix blue + red → purple. Blue + yellow → green. Red + yellow → orange. All three → brown.

The trick is proportions. A drop of indigo in a madder bath shifts red toward burgundy. A generous splash goes full purple.

modules.title: Recording mixes
modules.content:
Professional dyers record every mix. Without records you cannot repeat a colour — and clients hate inconsistency.

The record

  • Dye weights (in grams, per litre)
  • Mordant used and quantity
  • Temperature and time
  • Result photograph

A dyer's mix notebook is worth more than their dye stock. It captures years of experimentation.

modules.title: Match the mix to the colour

steps.q: You want a deep purple for a fashion commission. Which two dyes?
steps.f: Blue + red = purple. Indigo + madder is the classic purple pairing.

steps.q: You want a rich green. Which two dyes?
steps.f: Blue + yellow = green. Indigo + turmeric gives a rich, deep green.

steps.q: You want a warm earthy brown. Which dye approach?
steps.f: All three primaries combined give brown — the ratio controls the exact tone.

modules.title: Match a client's exact colour
modules.prompt: A client brings a fabric swatch of deep burgundy and asks you to dye a Gara cloth to match. Describe your process — from swatch analysis to final dye recipe.
modules.context: Exact colour matching is a premium service and a common requirement for export orders.
rubric: Analyses the swatch — determines primary dye proportions
Runs test dyeings with candidate recipes
Compares test dyeings to swatch under identical lighting
Refines recipe iteratively (small adjustments)
Documents the final recipe for reproduction

modules.title: Build a colour recipe book
modules.prompt: Create a personal colour recipe book with 10 named colours, each with its exact mix (grams per litre), mordant, temperature, time, and a photograph of the resulting swatch.
steps: Choose 10 distinct target colours
Develop a recipe for each
Produce and photograph a swatch for each
Record the exact recipe alongside the photo
Name each colour (e.g., 'Kono Deep Blue', 'Bo Burgundy')

skillDomains.name: Production & Quality
skillDomains.description: Move from single pieces to repeatable, professional-scale output.

modules.title: One is a hobby, ten is a business
modules.content:
Making one beautiful cloth is craft. Making fifty identical beautiful cloths is production — and it is a different discipline.

Scaling means:

  • Standardising — every step must be repeatable
  • Recording — so you can reproduce, delegate, and price
  • Splitting — one person measures, one ties, one dyes

Most Gara craftspeople fail to scale because they treat every cloth as unique. Consistency, not uniqueness, is what pays reliably.

modules.title: The standard recipe
modules.content:
A standard recipe is the foundation of any scalable Gara workshop. It specifies:

  • Exact fabric length/width per item
  • Exact tie layout (diagrammed)
  • Exact dye mix (grams per litre)
  • Exact dip schedule
  • Exact finishing (rinse, dry, iron)

Anyone trained on the recipe should be able to produce an item indistinguishable from any other made to the same recipe.

steps.q: Each table runner needs 100ml of dye at 1g/L concentration. You're making 20 runners. How much indigo powder total?
steps.f: 100ml × 20 = 2000ml = 2L. At 1g/L that's 2g total.

steps.q: Each dip takes 15 minutes plus 15 minutes aeration. 3 dips per cloth, 5 cloths in the vat at once. Total time for one full batch of 5?
steps.f: 3 dips × (15 dye + 15 air) = 90 minutes per batch of 5.

steps.q: Fabric costs 5,000 Le per metre. Each runner uses 1.2m. You're making 20. Total fabric cost?

modules.title: Plan a 50-piece batch
modules.prompt: You've won a contract to produce 50 identical medium-indigo table runners in 3 weeks. Describe your production plan — fabric sourcing, staffing, daily output schedule, quality checkpoints, and contingency for the vat failing.
modules.context: Real contracts require planning, not hope.
rubric: Calculates total fabric needed and sources it
Breaks production into daily targets
Assigns roles (if working with others)
Includes quality checkpoints at multiple stages
Addresses contingency — what happens if the vat fails or fabric is late
Identifies a buffer against the 3-week deadline

modules.title: Write your production SOP
modules.prompt: Write a complete Standard Operating Procedure for producing 20 identical table runners. Include recipes, tie diagrams, dip schedule, quality checks, and finishing standards.
steps: Define the exact product (dimensions, colour, pattern)
Document the tie layout with a diagram
Document the dye recipe and dip schedule
List quality checkpoints
List finishing standards (edges, ironing, folding)
Include a version number and date

skills.name: Quality Control
skills.description: Catch defects before the client sees them.

modules.title: Quality is what the client sees
modules.content:
Quality is not how hard you worked. Quality is what the client sees when they unfold the cloth.

Four quality dimensions matter most in Gara:

  • Colour — even, correct depth, no blotches
  • Pattern — crisp edges, clear intent, matches the brief
  • Finish — clean edges, no loose threads, ironed flat
  • Consistency — matches the sample the client approved

Each dimension must be checked before the cloth leaves your workshop.

modules.title: The three-point quality check
modules.content:
Every finished cloth passes through three checkpoints:

  1. Colour check — hold cloth beside reference swatch under natural light. Confirm match within tolerance.
  2. Pattern check — verify pattern matches the approved sample. Look for bleeding, missing ties, uneven spacing.
  3. Finish check — inspect for loose threads, stains, wrinkles, edge fraying.

Rejected cloths are reworked or sold as seconds — never shipped as firsts.

steps.q: You find blotchy, uneven colour across a cloth. Most likely cause?
o: Uneven dye absorption due to poor fabric prep or overcrowded vat
steps.f: Blotches come from sizing left in fabric or overcrowding the vat so dye can't reach all surfaces.

steps.q: Your pattern has feathered, fuzzy edges instead of sharp lines. What happened?
steps.f: Loose ties allow dye to bleed under them. Tighten for sharp edges.

steps.q: A finished cloth shows pale streaks near the fold. What's the diagnosis?
o: Dye couldn't penetrate the tight fold — tie was too thick or dipped too briefly
steps.f: Tight folds resist dye. Either tie less tightly or dip longer with more aeration.

modules.title: Build a quality system for your workshop
modules.prompt: Design a quality control system for a workshop producing 50 items per week. Describe the checkpoints, the acceptance criteria, and how you handle rejected pieces.
modules.context: Export buyers expect documented QC. Without it, you lose orders.
rubric: Identifies multiple checkpoints (incoming fabric, in-process, final)
Defines acceptance criteria per defect type
Assigns responsibility for each checkpoint
Describes what happens to rejected pieces (rework, seconds, reject)
Includes documentation (QC log per batch)

modules.title: Write a QC checklist
modules.prompt: Create a one-page QC checklist that any workshop employee can use to inspect finished cloths before they leave the workshop.
steps: List every quality dimension (colour, pattern, finish, consistency)
Define a pass/fail criterion for each
Include a photo of good vs defective examples where possible
Add a sign-off line for the inspector's name and date
Test the checklist on 10 finished pieces and refine

skillDomains.name: Business & Market
skillDomains.description: Turn craft skill into a working business that pays reliably.

skills.name: Costing & Pricing
skills.description: Know your costs. Price for profit.

modules.title: The four costs
modules.content:
Every Gara cloth has four costs:

  1. Materials — fabric, dye, thread, mordant
  2. Labour — your time at a fair hourly rate
  3. Overhead — workshop rent, electricity, water, tools
  4. Margin — profit to reinvest or live on

Beginners forget labour and overhead. They sell at cost and call it profit. Then they wonder why the workshop doesn't grow.

modules.title: The pricing formula
modules.content:
The standard formula:

Price = (Materials + Labour + Overhead) × (1 + Margin%)

Example

  • Materials: 12,000 Le
  • Labour: 4 hours × 2,500 Le/h = 10,000 Le
  • Overhead: 800 Le
  • Base: 22,800 Le
  • 35% margin: 30,780 Le

Quote 30,800 Le. Round to a clean number, but never round down below the formula's result.

steps.q: Materials 8,000 Le, Labour 3h × 2,000 Le = 6,000 Le, Overhead 500 Le, Margin 25%. What's the price?
You quote 30,000 Le. Materials cost 10,000, Labour 5,000, Overhead 2,000. What margin % is built in?
A client offers 20,000 Le for a cloth with 15,000 Le base cost and a 30% target margin (19,500 Le minimum). Accept?
o: Only if scope changes or it opens future business
steps.f: 20,000 / 15,000 = 1.33 → 33% margin. Marginal — accept only if there's a strategic reason.

modules.title: Handle a cost squeeze
modules.prompt: Your fabric supplier raises prices 20%. Your biggest client refuses a price increase. You have 6 months of orders at the old price. What do you do?
modules.context: Margin squeezes are the most common business problem in craft enterprises.
rubric: Calculates the new base cost per item
Identifies options: renegotiate supplier, find alternate supplier, increase efficiency, reduce materials waste
Considers client conversation — phased increase, added value, or scope adjustment
Plans a clear decision point (e.g., 2 months of data before deciding)
Considers diversification to reduce single-client dependency

modules.title: Build your price list
modules.prompt: Create a full price list for 8 standard Gara products (napkins, table runners, scarves, wall art, etc.), each with materials, labour, overhead, and margin calculations shown.
steps: Define 8 standard products
Calculate materials cost per product
Estimate labour hours and cost per product
Allocate overhead (rent, utilities, depreciation) per product
Apply a consistent margin target
Publish the final price list as a formal document

skills.name: Marketing & Sales
skills.description: Find buyers, price to the market, and communicate the value.

modules.title: Selling is telling the story
modules.content:
Gara sells on story as much as craft. A buyer in Freetown or Lagos or London is buying:

  • The cloth itself
  • The heritage behind the pattern
  • The maker (you) — their story, workshop, and skills

Marketing is not advertising. Marketing is telling the story clearly, repeatedly, to the right people.

modules.title: Know your three customers
modules.content:
Every Gara business has at least three customer types:

  1. Local individual buyers — market, church, family events. Price-sensitive but high volume.
  2. Local institutional buyers — hotels, schools, NGOs. Higher budget, larger orders, formal.
  3. Export buyers — boutiques, museums, individual collectors. Highest price, lowest volume, most demanding on quality.

You cannot serve all three well at the same time. Pick your priority and design your business around it.

modules.title: Match the marketing to the customer

steps.q: You want a hotel contract. What's the most effective outreach?
o: Direct visit with a physical sample and price list
steps.f: Institutional buyers expect professionalism. In-person with a physical portfolio and price list wins contracts.

steps.q: You want tourists walking by to buy. Best approach?
o: Visible display at point of sale with clear pricing
steps.f: Tourists buy on impulse — visible display, clear pricing, and story on the tag converts.

steps.q: You want an export boutique in Paris. What's the first step?
o: Research the boutique, prepare a professional lookbook, and email with samples by arrangement
Wait for them to find you
steps.f: Export buyers need to see a professional lookbook and understand your production capacity before committing.

modules.title: Write a 90-day marketing plan
modules.prompt: Your workshop can produce 80 cloths per month. You currently sell 20. Write a 90-day marketing plan to close the gap — what channels, what content, what outreach, and what success metrics.
modules.context: Unused production capacity is a business failure, not a comfort.
rubric: Identifies priority customer segment
Lists 3+ specific outreach activities (e.g., 10 hotel visits, 2 trade shows, weekly Instagram posts)
Assigns weekly time budget to marketing
Defines measurable metrics (leads per week, conversion rate, repeat rate)
Includes a review point at 30 days to adjust

modules.title: Build a professional lookbook
modules.prompt: Create a digital and physical lookbook showcasing 12 of your best pieces with product descriptions, cultural context for each pattern, pricing bands, and ordering information.
steps: Photograph 12 finished pieces professionally
Write a short cultural note for each pattern
Include dimensions, materials, and lead time
Design the layout (digital PDF + printed copy)
Print 10 physical copies for institutional buyers

skills.name: Export & International Trade
skills.description: Sell across borders — with the paperwork that makes it legal and profitable.

modules.title: Export is not just shipping
modules.content:
Exporting a Gara cloth to Europe or North America involves:

  • Shipping logistics (air vs sea vs courier)
  • Customs documentation (commercial invoice, packing list, certificate of origin)
  • Payment terms (advance, letter of credit, net 30)
  • Compliance (labelling, textile content disclosure, sometimes customs codes)

Each of these can sink a shipment. Getting them right is a professional skill.

modules.title: Payment terms
modules.content:
Never ship before you're paid. The standard options:

  • 100% advance — safest for seller, hardest for buyer to accept
  • 50% advance, 50% on delivery — common for first orders
  • Letter of credit (L/C) — bank guarantees payment once documents are correct
  • Net 30 — buyer pays 30 days after delivery; only for established relationships

New buyers get 50/50 or L/C. Never net 30 for a buyer you haven't worked with for a year.

steps.q: Which document certifies where the goods were made?
steps.f: Certificate of Origin proves the country of manufacture — critical for duty rates.

steps.q: Which document lists every item shipped and its weight?
steps.f: Packing list details quantities, weights, and dimensions — needed for customs.

steps.q: A buyer asks for net 30 terms on a first order. What do you propose?
steps.f: New buyers get 50/50 or L/C. Net 30 is for established, proven relationships.

modules.title: Build an export cost model
modules.prompt: You've received an order for 100 cloths from a UK boutique at 25 GBP each. Build the full cost model from your workshop to their door — including production, packaging, freight, insurance, customs duties, and payment processing — and calculate your net margin.
modules.context: Export prices look large until you subtract every layer of cost.
rubric: Separates production cost from export cost
Includes packaging suitable for international shipping
Includes freight (air or sea) with per-unit allocation
Includes insurance (typically 1–2% of value)
Accounts for buyer's customs duties (if DDP terms) or excludes clearly (if FOB)
Calculates net margin after all costs

modules.title: Assemble an export-ready pack
modules.prompt: Prepare the full document and pricing pack you'd send to a new international buyer: commercial invoice template, packing list template, certificate of origin procedure, shipping terms explanation, and pricing sheet in their currency.
steps: Create a commercial invoice template
Create a packing list template
Write the procedure for obtaining a Certificate of Origin
Write a one-page explanation of your Incoterms (FOB or DDP)
Produce a pricing sheet in the buyer's currency
Test the pack by having a mentor review it

capstoneAssessment.title: Capstone — Full Commission from Brief to Delivery
capstoneAssessment.description: Complete one full professional commission end-to-end: receive a client brief, design a pattern, produce the cloth to standard, price it correctly, and deliver with documentation.

requiredVisuals.purpose: Show finished cloth with detail views of the pattern
Show the fabric before dyeing and the finished cloth
Document every step taken from brief to delivery

stages: Stage 1: Client intake — capture the brief, occasion, colours, deadline, and budget in writing
Stage 2: Design — produce a sketch and one sample swatch; get client approval
Stage 3: Production — apply the full tie and dye process per your SOP
Stage 4: Quality — run the 3-point QC; address any defects
Stage 5: Pricing — calculate the final price using the standard formula; present the invoice
Stage 6: Delivery — package, document, deliver, and confirm client satisfaction in writing

rubric.criterion: Client brief captured accurately and in writing
Design matches the brief and cultural appropriateness of motifs
Craft quality — even colour, crisp pattern, clean finish
Delivery on time and to the client's satisfaction

implementationNotes: All lessons should be readable at two levels — beginner-friendly prose plus a deeper technical layer for returning learners
Each simulation level should be passable only when the learner demonstrates the specific skill the level tests
Drills and scenarios should be shuffled so learners can't memorise answer order
The capstone must be instructor-signed for the diploma to be awarded
Practical evidence (photographs of work) should be stored in the learner's portfolio and reviewable by an instructor
All images should be generated as SVG illustrations in the FuturePath visual style (dark background, accent green, technical diagram aesthetic)
Every module should reference at least one visual where possible — the certificate requires proof of work
